Okay. All right. So this is a map of his conquest. This is a burning of Pipulus, which you can still visit today in Iran. While his conquest was underway, he was slowly killing off his father's most loyal men. Parmmen, who was Phil's top general, and Cletus were both killed by Alexander. Historically, these events are remembered as random acts of violence, but they were not. Alexander needed to eliminate his father's men to build his own empire.

Eventually, the other generals realized that they would be next. They conspired and poisoned him, leading to infighting among them and the creation of the Greek world divided into four major parts: Egypt, Macedon, Anatolia, and the Seucian Empire. Once most of the world was conquered, Greeks had to rule over many non-Greeks. To manage their empire, they built Greek cities to settle veterans, invited more Greeks, and recruited Persian bureaucrats for effective governance, as well as Jews.

Focusing on Egypt, historically a cultural capital that influenced Greece with science and math, Egyptians now questioned Greek rule. The Greeks needed to explain why they controlled Egypt, leading to the creation of cultural imperialism. They built similar Greek cities around the world with theaters, gymasia, and agoras. Greek art also spread globally.

In Alexandria, the library systemized all Greek knowledge into textbooks for global education. When Egyptians asked for original plays as a deposit, Athenians initially refused but eventually agreed. However, after receiving money, Athenians kept the scrolls, angering Greeks deeply.

The library of Alexandria was part of the Musead and symbolized the use of education as a tool to create cultural understanding, enabling empire rule. The library exemplified Greek efforts to control Egypt through knowledge and culture.
